credit.title: About this guide
credit.text: An original guide by Lover of Sahara, written from our own field experience and from public sources: tourism boards, the Iriqui National Park, scientific studies and local operators. Information may change: conditions in the desert depend on the season and the weather.

items.intro-lead: Most visitors to the Moroccan Sahara never leave the tarmac. Erg Chegaga begins exactly where the tarmac ends: a vast, quiet sea of golden sand that can only be reached by 4x4, far from the crowds, the buses and the noise.

why.title: Why Chegaga
why.body:
Erg Chegaga is the largest dune field in Morocco, a belt of sand roughly 35 to 40 km long that lies beyond M'Hamid El Ghizlane, the last town on the road. There is no tarmac to the dunes. The final stretch is an off-road track of about 50 to 60 km, covered in around two hours by 4x4 over stony plains, dry riverbeds and soft sand.

That distance is what protects the place. The camps are few, small and far apart, the nights are truly dark and the silence is complete. This is the Sahara before the tourist road reached it, and it is the reason we take travellers here.

It also changes the way you travel. Getting to Chegaga is part of the experience: the changing landscapes, the last oasis, the first dunes, the sunset on the hammada. You do not arrive in the desert, you cross towards it.

chebbi.title: A word about Erg Chebbi
chebbi.body:
Erg Chebbi, near Merzouga, is spectacular too. Its dunes rise to about 150 m next to a paved road, which is exactly why it is so popular. In high season it hosts hundreds of camps, quad bikes and groups arriving by the busload. Many travellers love its comfort and its easy access.

Chegaga trades that convenience for space. If what you are looking for is solitude, a sky full of stars and the feeling of being a long way from everything, the extra kilometres are worth it.

items.compare-note: Figures come from public sources and tour-operator estimates and are indicative. Dune heights and distances vary from one source to another.

dunes.title: A great sea of sand
dunes.body:
An erg is a sand sea: a wide area of dunes built and rebuilt by the wind. Chegaga is more spread out than tall. Estimates for its highest dunes range from about 50 m to around 300 m depending on the source, but the real spectacle is the extent: ridge after ridge of golden sand, broken by dark gravel plains, small oases and patches of acacia.

Because the wind keeps reshaping the crests, no two visits show exactly the same landscape. Footprints disappear in a few hours.

light.title: Light, colour and silence
light.body:
The best hours are the first and the last of the day. At dawn the crests are sharp and cool in colour. At sunset the sand turns orange, then rose, then violet. In between, the midday sun is strong and bright, which is why walks are planned for the early morning and the late afternoon.

Away from roads and villages, the silence is striking. Often the only sounds are the wind, a camel's bell or the crackle of a fire.

camps.title: Camps at the edge of the dunes
camps.body:
Camps in Chegaga are usually small clusters of tents set among the dunes, far from each other. Bedding, meals and drinking water are normally provided by the camp. Because they depend on the 4x4 tracks and on the weather, they operate mainly from October to April, and they should be booked in advance.

In winter the nights are cold. Dinner by the fire, mint tea and music under the stars are part of the evening.

tamegroute.title: Tamegroute
tamegroute.body: The last stop before the desert is Tamegroute, known for its green-glazed pottery and for the Naciria zaouia, a Sufi centre whose library keeps rare ancient manuscripts. A good place to see craftsmen at work and to understand the spiritual and trading history of the Draa valley.

mhamid.title: M'Hamid El Ghizlane
mhamid.body: The last oasis of the Draa and the last town with a paved road. Its name refers to gazelles, and it was formerly known as Taragalt, the plain of gazelles. For centuries it was a gathering point for the caravans that left for Timbuktu. Today it is the place to stock up on water, meet the drivers and guides, and see the old ksar. Each autumn it hosts the Taragalte nomad culture festival.

hammada.title: The hammada and the track
hammada.body: Past the village the tarmac stops. The track crosses the hammada, a stony, flat desert plain, then dry riverbeds, thorny acacias and the first patches of sand. Depending on the season and the camp, the drive takes around two hours for about 50 to 60 km. A local driver who knows the tracks is essential: they shift with the wind and the rare rains.

arrival.title: Arrival in Chegaga
arrival.body: The first high dunes appear on the horizon like a golden wall. After the long drive, the arrival at camp is simple and powerful: mint tea, a walk up the nearest crest to watch the sunset, then dinner under a sky full of stars.

items.beyond-lead: Around Erg Chegaga, a few places are worth discovering for themselves. Each of them tells a different story of the desert: water, life, silence.

lihoudi.title: Erg Lihoudi
lihoudi.body:
Erg Lihoudi is the gentle introduction to the dunes: a compact field of sand about 7 to 10 km from M'Hamid (sources vary), reachable in around an hour by camel. Locally its name is said to mean the dune of the Jews. Its dunes are smaller and easier than those of Chegaga, perfect for a first walk at sunset or a first night in a bivouac.

Many itineraries stop here for lunch before continuing to Chegaga. It is also a good option for travellers with limited time.

oasis.title: The Sacred Oasis
oasis.body:
Out on the stony plain on the way to Chegaga, an unexpected island of green appears: a palm and acacia oasis fed by a natural spring that rises from the rock. Operators identify it with the Oum Laalag oasis, reported about 50 km south-west of M'Hamid and roughly 15 hectares in size. For the nomads it is a holy place. It has a shrine to a holy man, and local belief says that a fairy lives at its source.

The spring has always been vital: nomads still bring their animals to drink there, and caravans on the old road towards Timbuktu relied on it. Treat it as a place of worship. Ask your guide before entering or photographing the shrine.

iriki.title: Lake Iriki
iriki.body:
At the end of the Draa river, in a closed basin between the Jbel Bani and the dunes, lies Lake Iriki (also written Iriqui). For centuries the floods of the Atlas ran down the Draa and ended here. Since the dams were built upstream, the lake is dry most years: a flat, pale, cracked salt pan that is a landscape in itself, crossed by the old Foum Zguid to M'Hamid track.

When exceptional rains come, water returns within days, and so do the birds. Greater flamingos and waders have been recorded on the lake soon after floods; the most recent big flood reported was in September 2024. A 2025 scientific study describes the lake's revival after more than half a century of drying out. The water does not last, so never plan a trip around it: see it as a rare gift.

items.park-lead: The dunes of Chegaga lie on the edge of the Iriqui National Park, one of the largest protected areas in Morocco. The desert looks empty, but it is alive for those who know where to look.

park.title: Iriqui National Park
park.body: Created in 1994, the Iriqui National Park covers about 123,000 hectares across the provinces of Zagora and Tata. It protects the Iriki basin, the plains, the acacia valleys and part of the dune system, and is home to desert species that are increasingly rare in North Africa. Most animals are nocturnal and shy: the best way to meet them is to read the tracks in the sand at dawn.

gazelle.title: Dorcas gazelle
gazelle.body: The emblem of the area, and the origin of the name M'Hamid El Ghizlane. This small, elegant gazelle is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN: hunting and drought have reduced its numbers. It can survive on the moisture of plants and acacia leaves and rarely needs to drink.

fennec.title: Fennec fox
fennec.body: The smallest of all foxes, with huge ears that release heat. It is nocturnal and spends the day in a burrow in the sand. You are unlikely to see it, but its small tracks around the camp at dawn are a good sign. Golden jackals and other foxes are also reported in the park.

ostrich.title: The return of the ostrich
ostrich.body: The North African ostrich had almost disappeared from Morocco. In February 2023 the water and forests agency released 16 ostriches in the Iriqui National Park, and in 2024 the first nest in the wild was recorded. A reintroduction programme is still fragile, so please keep a distance if you see one.

houbara.title: Houbara bustard
houbara.body: A discreet ground bird, perfectly camouflaged, which is endangered because of hunting for falconry. It is one of the species that conservationists watch most closely in the region.

reptiles.title: Reptiles and small mammals
reptiles.body: The spiny-tailed lizard, a vegetarian that basks on warm rocks; the sidewinding Saharan horned viper, which leaves J-shaped tracks; jerboas, small jumping rodents that get all their water from their food; and the sandfish skink, which seems to swim in the sand. Shake out your shoes in the morning and look where you put your hands.

sky.title: A sky full of stars
sky.body:
With no towns for dozens of kilometres and only a few small camps, Chegaga's night sky is very dark. On a night without moon, the Milky Way casts a visible band across the sky and shooting stars are frequent. Winter air is dry and clear, which makes the view even better.

What helps: wait 20 to 30 minutes for your eyes to adapt, avoid using the phone light, choose the nights around the new moon, and dress warmly: winter nights can approach 0 °C. A blanket on the sand beyond the camp lights is the best seat there is.

In the morning, climb the nearest crest before sunrise. Watching the sun rise over the dunes after a night under the stars is the moment most travellers remember.

people.title: People of the desert
people.body:
Amazigh nomadic families still live in this region, moving with their goats and camels along tracks and wells their grandparents knew. The old caravans left M'Hamid for Timbuktu, and the traces of that trade can still be seen in the ksour, the wells and the shrines. Tea is the language of hospitality: three glasses, poured from a height, are shared slowly.

If you are invited into a tent, accept the tea. Ask before photographing people, and be generous in return, with time as much as with money.

doing.title: What to do
doing.body:
Camel trek between Lihoudi and Chegaga, or a short ride at sunset.
Drive across the dunes with an experienced driver.
Sandboarding on the steepest slopes.
Walk the crests at dawn and dusk.
Stargaze from the dunes.
Visit a nomad family and share tea.
See Lake Iriki and the Sacred Oasis.
Some camps also offer quad rides; if silence matters to you, ask before booking.
In late October, the Taragalte festival gathers musicians and nomad families in M'Hamid.

items.practical-lead: A few simple rules make the difference between a good trip and a great one.

water.title: Water and sun
water.body: Even in winter the desert sun is strong. Carry a reusable bottle (camps normally provide filtered water), wear a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses, apply sunscreen, and start walks early. Never leave the camp alone on foot without telling your guide.

pack.title: What to pack
pack.body:
Warm layers for the night: fleece or light down jacket, windproof layer, hat, warm socks.
Sun protection: SPF 50+, sunglasses, wide-brimmed hat.
A scarf (chèche) for sun and sand.
Closed shoes for the dunes, sandals for camp.
A soft bag, not a rigid suitcase: the last 50 to 60 km are by 4x4.
A power bank, a head torch, wet wipes and dust protection for your camera.
Some cash in dirhams: there are no payment terminals in the desert.

responsible.title: Travel lightly
responsible.body: Take all your rubbish with you, including cigarette ends and wet wipes. Stay on existing tracks to protect the fragile plain. Do not disturb wildlife or take plants, fossils or stones. Respect shrines and sacred places. Ask before photographing people. Leave the dunes as you found them: clean, and silent.

items.us-lead: Our work is simple: take curious travellers to the real Sahara, by 4x4, and leave the crowds behind. These are some of our trips to Erg Chegaga and Erg Lihoudi.

us.title: How we travel
us.body: Our trips stay away from the main tourist roads: we cross the hammada by 4x4, stop in Tamegroute and in the oasis, and reach the dunes at the right hour of light. Tell us how many days you have and where you start from, and we will build the route with you.

journey-text.title: From the last oasis to the dunes
journey-text.body:
From Zagora, the road follows the Draa valley south through palm groves and ksour. Tamegroute is a natural first stop; M'Hamid El Ghizlane is the last place to buy water and supplies. Beyond the village, the tarmac gives way to a track.

The track is not a single road: it is a network of paths across the hammada, the dry riverbeds and the plains, chosen by the drivers according to the weather. After about two hours the first dunes of Erg Chegaga appear on the horizon. If you come from Foum Zguid, the old track crosses the dry bed of Lake Iriki; from M'Hamid, it passes the Sacred Oasis.

Some good habits for the trip: leave early to arrive with the afternoon light, travel with water and a full tank, and never go alone. A single 4x4 and no network is not a plan; a local driver who knows the tracks is the safest and the most interesting way to go.

What to expect
rows: Warm, comfortable days and the start of the camp season. A first wind and sand window is possible in October.
